lessons.title: Following instructions and school rules
lessons.objective: Listen to and follow instructions in order, and explain why school rules matter.
lessons.course:
Instructions tell us what to do, often in order: First, take out your book. Next, open it at page 10. Then, read the title. Finally, close the book.
School rules help everybody learn safely: come on time, respect others, keep the school clean, do not fight.
lessons.model: The teacher gives three instructions; Bih repeats them in order before doing them.
lessons.guided: Listen to a set of four instructions, repeat them, then do them. Discuss: which school rule do you find most useful, and why?
lessons.exercise: What word starts the last instruction?
lessons.remediation: Give two instructions at a time.
lessons.transfer: Give three instructions to a younger child and check that they are followed.

practice.prompt: Put the instructions in order.
Listen and do the instructions in order.
practice.listen: First, stand up. Next, touch your nose. Then, turn around. Finally, sit down.
practice.answer: Stand up, touch your nose, turn around, sit down.

practice.prompt: Why do schools have rules?
choices: so that everybody can learn safely
practice.answer: so that everybody can learn safely

lessons.title: A rhyme about school and its lesson
lessons.objective: Read and say a rhyme, find the rhyming words, put oneself in the place of the speaker and deduce the lesson.
lessons.course: A rhyme has lines that end with the same sound. It often teaches a lesson. We read it with rhythm, then we ask: Who speaks? How does he feel? What does the rhyme teach?

support.title: Klassia rhyme
support.text:
I was late, I ran too fast,
I fell and came to school the last.
Now I wake when the cock crows loud,
I walk with care and join the crowd.

lessons.model: The adult reads the rhyme with rhythm and stresses the rhyming words: fast – last, loud – crowd.
lessons.guided: Read the rhyme together. Find the rhyming pairs. Imagine you are the child in the rhyme: what will you do tomorrow?
lessons.remediation: Read two lines at a time and clap the rhythm.
lessons.transfer: Say the rhyme to your family and explain its lesson.

practice.prompt: Match the rhyming words.
practice.explanation: Rhyming words end with the same sound.

practice.prompt: What lesson does the rhyme teach?
choices: Wake up early so you are not late.
Run as fast as you can.
practice.answer: Wake up early so you are not late.
practice.explanation: The child now wakes up early and walks with care.

practice.prompt: Listen to the rhyme and say it after the voice.
practice.listen: I was late, I ran too fast, I fell and came to school the last. Now I wake when the cock crows loud, I walk with care and join the crowd.

lessons.title: A descriptive paragraph: my school
lessons.objective: Write a descriptive text of about 60 words about one’s school.
lessons.course:
A description has an opening sentence (what we describe), some sentences with details (what we see, how many, what colour, where), and a closing sentence (what we feel).
We use adjectives and linking words. About 60 words is five or six short sentences.

support.title: Useful words
support.text: classrooms, playground, flag, trees, headmaster’s office, clean, large, noisy, friendly

lessons.model: “My school is in Nkwen. It has six classrooms painted blue. In front of the office, the flag flies every morning. Mango trees give shade in the playground. During break, the pupils play football and skip. I love my school because my teachers are kind.”
lessons.guided: Plan with three boxes: opening, details, closing. Write a sentence in each box, then add details.
lessons.exercise: Write the opening sentence of your description.
lessons.answer: For example: My school is in Nkwen.
lessons.remediation: Complete a gapped model text before writing your own.
lessons.transfer: Describe your house in about 60 words.
lessons.materials: Paper, a plan with three boxes.

practice.prompt: Write your description of about 60 words.
practice.answer: A description with an opening, details and a closing sentence.

practice.prompt: Put the parts of a description in order.
practice.explanation: This is the plan of a description.

practice.prompt: Which sentence is a good closing sentence?
choices: I love my school because my teachers are kind.
practice.answer: I love my school because my teachers are kind.
practice.explanation: A closing sentence says what we feel.

lessons.title: Verbs: present, past and future
lessons.objective: Use regular and irregular verbs in the simple present, simple past and simple future.
lessons.course:
Simple present (every day): I walk to school. She walks to school.
Simple past (yesterday): regular verbs add -ed: walk → walked, play → played. Irregular verbs change: go → went, eat → ate, write → wrote, come → came.
Simple future (tomorrow): will + verb: I will walk. They will write.
lessons.model: The adult says: “Every day I go to school. Yesterday I went to school. Tomorrow I will go to school.”
lessons.guided: Make a table with three columns: today, yesterday, tomorrow. Put five verbs in each tense.
lessons.remediation: Practise regular verbs first, then learn three irregular verbs a day.
lessons.transfer: Tell what you did yesterday and what you will do tomorrow in two sentences.

practice.prompt: Complete with the past tense.
practice.text: Yesterday Bih [[went]] (go) to school and [[played]] (play) football.
practice.explanation: go is irregular (went); play is regular (played).

practice.prompt: Which one is in the future?
Match each verb with its past form.

lessons.title: Equal and equivalent sets
lessons.objective: Distinguish equal sets (same elements) from equivalent sets (same number of elements).
lessons.course:
Two sets are equal if they have exactly the same elements: {pen, ruler} = {ruler, pen}.
Two sets are equivalent if they have the same number of elements, even if the elements are different: {pen, ruler} and {Bih, Tabi} are equivalent (2 elements each). We write ↔ or say “equivalent”.
lessons.model: The adult shows {chalk, duster} and {duster, chalk}: equal. Then {chalk, duster} and {teacher, pupil}: equivalent, not equal.
lessons.guided: Make pairs of sets with school objects. Decide: equal, equivalent, or neither.
lessons.exercise: A = {a, b, c} and B = {x, y, z}. Are they equal or equivalent?
lessons.remediation: Count the elements of each set first.
lessons.transfer: Find two equivalent sets at home (for example 4 chairs and 4 people).

practice.prompt: {1, 2, 3} and {3, 2, 1}: equal or equivalent only?
practice.explanation: Same elements, so equal (and also equivalent).

practice.prompt: How many elements must B have to be equivalent to {red, blue, green, yellow}?
practice.explanation: Equivalent sets have the same number of elements.

practice.prompt: Complete: equal sets have the same ___.
practice.explanation: Equal sets have exactly the same elements.

lessons.title: Subtracting numbers up to 500
lessons.objective: Subtract numbers up to 500 with and without borrowing, and check with addition.
lessons.course:
We subtract in columns, starting with the units. If the top digit is smaller, we borrow 1 ten (or 1 hundred) from the next column.
  352
− 127
= 225
We check: 225 + 127 = 352.
lessons.model: The school has 352 pupils; 127 are in the lower classes. The adult subtracts: units 2 − 7 cannot, borrow: 12 − 7 = 5; tens 4 − 2 = 2; hundreds 3 − 1 = 2. Answer: 225.
lessons.guided: Do three subtractions in columns, then check each one with an addition.
lessons.exercise: A library has 420 books. 185 are borrowed. How many books are left?
lessons.transfer: Find how much money is left after a purchase.

practice.prompt: How can we check a subtraction?
choices: by adding the answer and the number taken away
practice.answer: by adding the answer and the number taken away

lessons.title: The calendar: months, ordinary and leap years
lessons.objective: Name the 12 months, know their number of days and distinguish ordinary and leap years.
lessons.course:
A year has 12 months. Some have 31 days (January, March, May, July, August, October, December), some have 30 (April, June, September, November). February has 28 days in an ordinary year and 29 in a leap year.
An ordinary year has 365 days; a leap year has 366 days and comes every four years (2024, 2028).
lessons.model: The adult shows the school calendar: “School resumes in September, which has 30 days.”
lessons.guided: Use your knuckles to remember the months of 31 days. Find the dates of school holidays on a calendar.
lessons.exercise: How many days are in a leap year?
lessons.remediation: Learn the months in order, then their days.
lessons.transfer: Find your birthday on the calendar and count the days until it comes.

practice.prompt: How many days does April have?
Which year is a leap year?
How many days in February in an ordinary year?

lessons.title: Tallying in 5s and a bar graph of the class
lessons.objective: Collect data, tally in groups of 5 and represent the data on a bar graph.
lessons.course:
To tally, we draw one stroke for each thing and cross every group of four with a fifth stroke: |||| crossed = 5. We count in 5s.
A bar graph shows the totals with bars of different heights. It has a title, labels and a scale.
lessons.model: The adult tallies how pupils come to school: walking 23, motorbike 8, car 4, bicycle 5.
lessons.guided: Ask 20 people a question (favourite subject). Tally the answers, then draw a bar graph.
lessons.exercise: How many strokes are in one tally group?
lessons.remediation: Tally with real objects in groups of five before drawing.
lessons.transfer: Make a bar graph of the fruits your family eats in a week.

practice.prompt: Four full tally groups and 3 strokes. How many?
Walking 23, motorbike 8, car 4, bicycle 5. Which is the most common way to come to school?
Draw the bar graph of how pupils come to school.
practice.answer: A bar graph with four bars and a title.

lessons.title: Toilets at school: types and care
lessons.objective: Identify types of toilets and care for the school toilet appropriately.
lessons.course:
There are different toilets: the pit latrine, the ventilated improved pit latrine (VIP) with a pipe that takes out bad smells, and the water-flush toilet.
We keep toilets clean: we use them correctly, we flush or cover the hole, we do not throw objects inside, we wash our hands with soap after.
lessons.model: The adult explains the school toilet: “This is a VIP latrine. The pipe takes the smell away. We cover the hole after use.”
lessons.guided: Visit the school toilet with the teacher. Make a class rota to keep it clean and a poster of the rules.
lessons.exercise: What do we do after using the toilet?
lessons.answer: We wash our hands with soap.
accept: we wash our hands with soap
We wash our hands with soap
lessons.remediation: Learn the three rules: use correctly, keep clean, wash hands.
lessons.transfer: Help to keep the toilet at home clean this week.

practice.prompt: Match each toilet with its feature.
practice.answer: pit: hole; VIP: vent pipe; flush: water.

practice.prompt: Which one should NOT go into a toilet?
Why must toilets be kept clean?
practice.answer: To prevent diseases and bad smells.

lessons.title: Lire un petit texte : à l’école
lessons.objective: Lire à haute voix un texte simple de quatre phrases et répondre à des questions sur ce texte.
lessons.course: On lit d’abord le titre, puis le texte, phrase par phrase. On s’arrête au point. On cherche les réponses dans le texte.

support.title: Lis le texte
support.text:
À l’école
La classe de Manka est grande. Le maître écrit au tableau. Les élèves lisent en silence. À la récréation, ils jouent au ballon.

lessons.model: L’adulte lit le texte à haute voix, puis demande : « Qui écrit au tableau ? »
lessons.guided: Lis le texte à haute voix deux fois. Réponds aux questions en recopiant les mots du texte.
lessons.remediation: Lis une phrase à la fois avec l’adulte.
lessons.transfer: Lis à ta famille une petite phrase en français que tu as écrite.

practice.prompt: Que font les élèves à la récréation ?
practice.explanation: Le texte dit : ils jouent au ballon.

practice.prompt: Remets les phrases dans l’ordre du texte.
items: La classe de Manka est grande.
À la récréation, ils jouent au ballon.

practice.prompt: Écoute le texte et lis-le à haute voix.
practice.listen: La classe de Manka est grande. Le maître écrit au tableau. Les élèves lisent en silence. À la récréation, ils jouent au ballon.
practice.answer: Le texte lu à haute voix.

lessons.title: Children’s rights and duties at school
lessons.objective: Identify children’s rights and duties and say what to do in case of abuse.
lessons.course:
Children have rights: education, health, a name, protection, play, to be heard. They also have duties: to respect others, to work at school, to follow rules, to help at home.
No adult or child may hurt a child. If someone hurts you or touches you in a way you do not like, say no, go away and tell a trusted adult.
lessons.model: The teacher explains: “You have the right to learn. You have the duty to come on time and to respect your classmates.”
lessons.guided: Make two lists: my rights / my duties. Name three trusted adults you can tell if something is wrong.
lessons.exercise: Name one duty of a pupil.
lessons.answer: For example: to come to school on time.
lessons.remediation: Match each right with its duty: right to learn — duty to work.
lessons.transfer: Talk with your parents about your rights and your duties at home.

practice.prompt: Match each right with a duty that goes with it.
Someone hurts you. What do you do?
choices: say no, go away and tell a trusted adult
practice.answer: say no, go away and tell a trusted adult

practice.prompt: Name one trusted adult at school.
practice.answer: For example: the teacher or the head teacher.

lessons.title: Stitches and sewing on a button
lessons.objective: Make simple stitches (running stitch) and sew on a button safely.
lessons.course:
Needlework tools: needle, thread, thimble, scissors, pins. A running stitch goes in and out of the cloth in a straight line. To sew a button: thread the needle, tie a knot, pass the needle through the holes several times, then tie the thread under the cloth.
We keep needles and pins in a pin cushion and work carefully.
lessons.model: The adult shows a running stitch on a piece of cloth, then sews a button on a school shirt.
lessons.guided: Practise a row of running stitches on a piece of cloth. Then sew a big button with the adult.
lessons.exercise: Where do we keep needles and pins?
lessons.remediation: Practise with a big needle and thick thread on paper with holes.
lessons.transfer: Sew back a button on a piece of clothing at home with an adult.
lessons.materials: Needle, thread, cloth, buttons, scissors (with an adult).

practice.prompt: Put the steps for sewing a button in order.
items: Pass the needle through the holes.
Tie the thread under the cloth.
practice.answer: thread, knot, pass through the holes, tie.

practice.prompt: Which fastening has teeth that close?
Draw a row of running stitches.
practice.explanation: In and out, in a straight line.

lessons.title: Acting a sketch about school life
lessons.objective: Act roles following a short script and perform with expression.
lessons.course: A sketch is a short play. Each actor has a role and says his lines in turn. We speak loudly and clearly, we face the audience, we use gestures and facial expressions. Some scenes are silent (mime): the body tells the story.

support.title: Short script
support.text:
TEACHER: Good morning, class. Where is your homework, Tabi?
TABI (looking in his bag): I am sorry, madam. I left it at home.
TEACHER: Bring it tomorrow, please.
TABI: Yes, madam. Thank you.

lessons.model: Two adults act the script: one is the teacher, one is Tabi. They show the feelings with the face.
lessons.guided: Learn one role, act the sketch with a partner, then act a silent version with mime only.
lessons.exercise: What is a short play called?
lessons.remediation: Say only one line, with a gesture.
lessons.transfer: Act the sketch for your family.
lessons.materials: The script, a few simple props.

practice.prompt: Which behaviour helps an actor?
choices: speak loudly and face the audience
turn his back to the audience
practice.answer: speak loudly and face the audience
practice.explanation: The audience must see and hear.

practice.prompt: Put the lines of the script in order.
items: Good morning, class. Where is your homework, Tabi?
I am sorry, madam. I left it at home.

practice.prompt: Act the sketch with a partner.

lessons.title: Relay races: touch and run, zigzag, shuttle
lessons.objective: Take part in relay races and pass the baton correctly.
lessons.course:
In a relay, a team runs in turns. In “touch and run” the next runner leaves when touched. In a zigzag relay we run around cones. In a shuttle relay we run to a line and back.
To pass the baton: the runner holds it out; the next runner takes it without stopping.
lessons.model: The adult and a child show a baton pass: “Hand out, take it, run!”
lessons.guided: Make teams of four. Run a zigzag relay and a shuttle relay; practise passing the baton.
lessons.remediation: Practise the baton pass while walking.
lessons.transfer: Play a relay game with friends.

practice.prompt: Match each relay with its rule.
pairs: run to a line and back
practice.answer: touch: leave; zigzag: cones; shuttle: back and forth.

practice.prompt: Four runners each run 25 m. How many metres for the team?
How do we pass the baton?
choices: hold it out and the next runner takes it running
practice.answer: hold it out and the next runner takes it running

lessons.title: Family words and the letters of our alphabet
lessons.objective: Say the words for members of a nuclear family in the family language and recognise letters of the General Alphabet of Cameroonian Languages.
lessons.course:
A nuclear family is the father, the mother and the children. Each language has its words for them.
The General Alphabet of Cameroonian Languages (GACL) gives letters to write our languages; some letters are not in the English alphabet, such as ɛ, ɔ and ŋ.
Klassia does not give the family words here: say them with your family, who know the language.
lessons.model: The adult says each family word in the family language and writes it, showing the special letters if there are any.
lessons.guided: Ask an adult the words for father, mother, brother and sister in the family language. Write them with the adult. Find special letters (ɛ, ɔ, ŋ).
lessons.exercise: Who are the members of a nuclear family?
lessons.answer: The father, the mother and the children.
accept: the father, the mother and the children
The father, the mother and the children
lessons.remediation: Start with two words: father and mother.
lessons.transfer: Make a family tree with the words in the family language.
lessons.materials: Paper, an adult who speaks the language.

practice.prompt: Which letter is NOT in the English alphabet?
practice.explanation: ŋ is a letter of the General Alphabet.

practice.prompt: Write the family words in the family language with an adult.
practice.answer: Family words written with the adult.
practice.explanation: Ask the adult to check the spelling.

practice.prompt: Draw your nuclear family and label each person.

lessons.title: Devices that need software
lessons.objective: Identify ICT devices that need software and explain simply how they function.
lessons.course:
Software is the set of programs that tell a device what to do. Computers, mobile telephones and tablets need software: an operating system to start, and applications (apps) to write, calculate, take photos or call.
Without software, the device is like a book with no words.
lessons.model: The adult switches on a phone: “The operating system starts. Then I open the calculator app.”
lessons.guided: With an adult, find three apps on a phone or a computer and say what each does.
lessons.exercise: What tells a device what to do?
lessons.remediation: Compare: a phone switched off and a phone with an app open.
lessons.transfer: Ask an adult which apps they use for work.
lessons.materials: A phone or a computer (with an adult).

practice.prompt: Match each app with what it does.
practice.answer: calculator: counts; camera: photos; word processor: texts.

practice.prompt: Which device needs software?
What starts first when a computer is switched on?
practice.explanation: It prepares the computer for apps.
